title: Predicted condensation-related signatures localize to two C-terminal regions of the prion protein across cervid PRNP variants associated with chronic wasting disease.
authors: Dayhoff, Guy W; Dorosh, Lyudmyla; Wille, Holger; Uversky, Vladimir N; Stepanova, Maria
abstract: Genetic variation in cervid PRNP influences chronic wasting disease (CWD) susceptibility and progression, but it remains unclear whether disease-associated substitutions produce localized differences in sequence-derived properties relevant to prion protein (PrPC) condensation. We compared a white-tailed deer (WTD) reference sequence with 10 modeled variants on the same mature PrP scaffold (residues 24-233). For each sequence, we calculated intrinsic disorder, FuzDrop per-residue droplet-promoting propensity (pDP) and binding-mode entropy (Sbind), predicted residue-level pKa values, and a discrete-charge summary at pH 7.0. The overall profiles preserve a long N-terminal droplet-promoting region, whereas variant-associated differences are concentrated in selected intervals. In the FuzDrop outputs, residues 126-140 show allele-dependent changes in pDP near the droplet-promoting threshold, and residues 220-230 show variant-specific changes in Sbind, including lower Sbind for S225F/Y and higher Sbind for elk-like Q226E. These differences occur without large changes in overall intrinsic disorder. KaML pKa predictions identify near-neutral titratable sites that provide electrostatic context for these local predictor differences. Independent atomistic simulations of monomeric PrP further detected variant-sensitive backbone behavior and intramolecular contacts involving these intervals. Together, the analysis identifies residues 126-140 and 220-230 as computationally defined candidate intervals that overlap regions implicated independently in prion conversion or CWD fibril structure, motivating direct tests of cervid PrP condensation and maturation.

title: Molecular Dynamics Insights into Biomineralization Mediated by Acidic Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: A Case Study of Molluscan Aspein from the Pearl Oyster Pinctada fucata.
authors: Mignon, Julien; Monari, Antonio; Longhi, Sonia; Michaux, Catherine
abstract: Biomineralization is a ubiquitous phenomenon that still fascinates the scientific community. Mineralized structures are most notably encountered in marine lifeforms, the shell or exoskeleton of which are formed by precipitating specific calcium carbonate (CaCO3) polymorphs, known as amorphous (ACC), vaterite, aragonite, and calcite. To control crystalline polymorphism in their shell layers, bivalves have evolved strategies involving ion-binding secretomes composed of shell matrix proteins (SMPs). Secreted in the prismatic layer of the pearl oyster Pinctada fucata, Aspein is an unusually acid-rich protein exclusively aspartic and famously recognized as the most acidic SMP known to date. Through in vitro crystallization experiments, Aspein was shown to select calcite over aragonite in modern seawater conditions. However, how it exerts its selectivity with respect to its structural properties remains enigmatic. By combining sequence-based predictions with all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we unveiled that Aspein is an intrinsically disordered organic matrix protein (IDOMP) undergoing ion-specific chain collapse and phase separation. Thanks to its unique Asp density and conformational fuzziness, Aspein first sequesters Ca2+ then attracts CO32- ions before stabilizing ACC and calcite-like phases, while precluding the incorporation of Mg2+ to avoid aragonite formation. Indeed, via Asp-Ca2+ bridges, the coalescence of structure-less clusters into supersaturated protein-CaCO3 assemblies promotes calcitic ordering. Therefore, Aspein plasticity, condensation susceptibility, and aspartic density critically modulate the pathway that defines CaCO3 polymorphism by inhibiting nucleation and controlling the growth of biogenic minerals. From a broader perspective, our study underpins some of the molecular and physicochemical principles governing biomineralization processes mediated by IDOMPs, the overlooked yet prevalent role of which was mechanistically unexplored.

title: Multiscale Molecular Simulations in the Age of Exascale Computing.
authors: Tan, Cheng; Sugita, Yuji
abstract: The interior of living cells is highly crowded with proteins, nucleic acids, and metabolites-a setting that simultaneously demands large system sizes and long simulation timescales. Exascale computing, now realized on modern supercomputers, offers a qualitatively new opportunity to address this challenge. In this review, we examine how multiscale molecular dynamics simulations-spanning all-atom, coarse-grained, and ultra-coarse-grained representations-are transforming our understanding of macromolecular crowding and liquid-liquid phase separation. We survey recent advances in force-field development, machine-learning-assisted system construction, and high-performance computing-optimized molecular dynamics engines, with particular attention to how these tools make large-scale simulations practically feasible. Key physical insights discussed include the interplay between excluded volume and nonspecific sticky interactions, crowding-induced slowdown of diffusion, metabolite-binding kinetics, and the regulatory mechanisms governing biomolecular condensate formation and maturation. We outline how exascale platforms, integrated with machine learning and experimental data, are bringing predictive whole-cell simulations within reach.

title: Molecular Dynamics Investigation of Human Endosulfatase HSulf-2 Reveals the Structural Roles of Intrinsically Disordered Regions, Catalytic Residues, and N-Glycosylation.
authors: Tao, Jianjun; Daniel, Regis; Basdevant, Nathalie
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Human endosulfatases HSulf-1 and HSulf-2 are the only extracellular sulfatases that selectively remove 6-O-sulfate groups from heparan sulfate chains, thereby regulating numerous signaling pathways involved in development, tissue homeostasis, and cancer. In particular, HSulf-2 is frequently overexpressed in human cancers, making it an attractive therapeutic target. However, its three-dimensional structure has not been resolved experimentally, mainly because of its multidomain organization, extensive post-translational modifications, and large intrinsically disordered hydrophilic domain (HD). Here, molecular dynamics simulations based on the AlphaFold2 model of HSulf-2 were used to investigate the structural and dynamic contributions of its domains and selected post-translational modifications. The simulations identified several intrinsically disordered regions, confirming that the HD constitutes the principal source of conformational disorder within the enzyme. They further demonstrate that the CAT-Cter assembly reproduces the canonical catalytic architecture conserved throughout the sulfatase family, whereas the HD induces only minor changes in the average structure while significantly destabilizing the conformational dynamics of the catalytic framework. In contrast, maturation of the catalytic residue modulates the conformational landscape of HSulf-2 without altering its overall architecture, whereas the conserved chitobiose cores of N-glycans exert only limited structural effects. These results support a modular structural organization in which the CAT-Cter assembly provides the conserved catalytic scaffold, while the HD confers the dynamic properties required for recognition of polymeric heparan sulfate substrates. This work provides a structural framework for understanding HSulf specificity and opens new perspectives for the rational design of selective HSulf inhibitors. In particular, the modular organization suggests that future dual-site inhibitors that simultaneously target the conserved catalytic pocket and the unique hydrophilic domain could combine high binding affinity with selectivity for HSulf enzymes.

title: Microfluidic Control of Biomolecular Condensate Growth Reveals Scaling Crossover and Interfacial Regulation.
authors: Lian, Xinyi; Yang, Fengchang; Guo, Yongjie; Yang, Chun; Wang, Leilei; Wang, Zheng; Zheng, Xu; Guan, Dongshi
abstract: Biomolecular condensates, formed via phase separation, play vital roles in cellular organization, yet their nucleation and growth dynamics remain poorly understood, particularly under controlled physiological conditions. Here, we employ a microfluidic platform to precisely manipulate the nucleation and growth of PGL-3 protein condensates at fluid-solid interfaces. We demonstrate that ionic strength and co-phase-separating proteins (SEPA-1) robustly tune the nucleation rate without altering the long-term growth scaling  approximately tn. Single-condensate tracking further resolves a dynamic scaling crossover from rapid isolated growth with n  approximately  1/2 to diffusion-limited collective growth with n  approximately  1/3, consistent with simulations of overlapping protein-depletion fields. Furthermore, we show that this classical scaling breaks down during viscoelastic phase separation, where elastic-dominated condensates exhibit a significantly reduced exponent. Our work establishes molecular modulation and interfacial mechanics as key regulators of condensate dynamics, revealing physical principles that govern the size and material state of biological condensates.

title: Metropolis and kinetic Monte Carlo methods for studying protein interactions.
authors: de Oliveira, Luciana Renata; Rodrigues, Luiz Fernando de Camargo; Itri, Rosangela
abstract: Protein-protein interactions are stochastic and play a central role in determining the structural and dynamic properties of biological systems. Computational approaches that account for the probabilistic nature of these interactions are therefore essential for understanding processes ranging from molecular self-assembly to biomolecular phase separation. Among these approaches, Monte Carlo (MC) methods have become important tools for investigating protein systems across multiple spatial and temporal scales. This review examines the application of MC simulations to protein-protein interactions, with particular emphasis on Metropolis Monte Carlo (MMC) and kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) methods as complementary approaches for investigating equilibrium properties and dynamic molecular processes. Applications ranging from receptor organization and protein aggregation to biomolecular condensation and liquid-liquid phase separation are discussed together with the evolution of coarse-grained models, from isotropic particles to anisotropic patchy particles and polymer representations that capture directional, multivalent, and sequence-dependent interactions. Finally, the integration of MC simulations with experimental techniques is reviewed through applications involving Small Angle X-ray and Neutron Scattering (SAXS/SANS), single-molecule tracking, and fluorescence-based methods, highlighting how experimentally accessible observables can be directly compared with simulation results to characterize protein interactions and estimate molecular parameters.

title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores.
authors: Yu, Miao; Heidari, Maziar; Palacio-Rodriguez, Karen; Ruan, Hao; Mingu, Sara; Chen, Yu; Gou, Xu-Zhuo; Shen, Pingkai; Liu, Songzi; Chen, Si-Yu; Hidayat, Alam Ahmad; Bode, Mathis; Sikora, Mateusz; Tang, Ai-Hui; Hummer, Gerhard; Lemke, Edward A
abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm(1,2). Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated(3-13). Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. By combining site-specific labelling with time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy, here we show that FG domains exhibit nanosecond-scale, liquid-like segmental motion in live cells, whereas reconstituted FG condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition in vitro. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-beta, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked beta-N-acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG-FG and FG-importin-beta interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-beta is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations(14) of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-beta in mammalian cells. Together, our results reconcile conflicting models of FG-NUP organization(4,5,7,9,15) and establish a framework for understanding how cellular context tunes intrinsically disordered proteins in health and disease.

title: MobiDB in 2027: machine-actionable access to intrinsic protein disorder knowledge.
authors: Piovesan, Damiano; Lamara, Abdeldjallil; Worth, Alison Mae; Mehdiabadi, Mahta; Begue, Sol C; Tosatto, Silvio C E
abstract: MobiDB (https://mobidb.org) integrates structural and functional annotations for intrinsically disordered proteins and regions across UniProtKB. The 2027 release strengthens semantic consistency, programmatic access, and reproducible reuse. A refined controlled vocabulary groups features in a hierarchical way and distinguishes evidence classes and types annotation sources as providers, methods, or aggregation rules. A new versioned REST API, along with a developed MCP server, enables scripts, workflows, and tool-using artificial intelligence systems to retrieve and combine evidence-bearing records through documented operations. The redesigned website applies the same vocabulary to protein entries, documentation, and cross-proteome statistics. Additional developments include standardized Nextflow production workflows, updated RING Protein Data Bank interaction processing, integration of Motif Map of the Proteome and Linear Motif mediated Protein-Protein Interaction Database annotations, and a release-aware catalogue of static datasets for large-scale analysis. Following the recent increase in reference proteomes in UniProtKB, MobiDB now provides a more representative estimate of long-disorder with a median residue coverage of 12.3% in eukaryotes, 1.9% in archaea, 1.7% in bacteria, and 3.4% in viruses; and protein prevalence of 48.7%, 11.9%, 11.2%, and 25.0%, respectively. Together, these developments make disorder knowledge easier to discover, relate to function, and reuse with explicit provenance.

title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis.
authors: Zeng, Wei; Lamelas, Laura; Scaramozzino, Domenico; Chen, Zhuo Angel; Rappsilber, Juri; Xue, Shuqin; Jaeger, Katja E; Orellana, Laura; Sampathkumar, Arun; Wigge, Philip A
abstract: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.

title: A mechanistic modeling framework for the rational design of aqueous two-phase systems targeting variant-specific biomolecules.
authors: Zhang, Yage; Siu, Ryan Ho-Ping; Liu, Sihan; Lei, Qifang; Tanner, Julian A; Binks, Bernard P; Guo, Wei; Shum, Ho Cheung
journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
abstract: HYPOTHESIS: The partitioning of biomolecules in aqueous two-phase systems (ATPS), a liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) process that biomimics cellular compartmentalization, is governed by quantifiable protein biophysical properties. Therefore, the partitioning behavior of uncharacterized biomolecular variants can be predicted mechanistically rather than optimized empirically. EXPERIMENTS: Using SARS-CoV-2 spike protein variants (wild type, Beta, Omicron, and the Omicron receptor-binding domain) as a model system, we combined process-intensified LLPS in an evaporating sessile droplets, tie-line-resolved phase diagram analysis, microfluidic picoliter-droplet partitioning assays, and polymer-engineered ATPS in which polyethylene glycol (PEG) was substituted with the more hydrophobic PEG-PPG-PEG triblock copolymer. AlphaFold3-based structural analysis, Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity and isoelectric point calculations were integrated with multivariate linear regression to link partition coefficients to protein properties. A Collander-type inter-system correlation was established to test transferability across ATPS formulations. FINDINGS: All spike protein variants preferentially partitioned into the dextran-rich phase, with enrichment amplified by longer tie-lines and further enhanced by the more hydrophobic PEG-PPG-PEG system, confirming hydrophobic interactions as the dominant partitioning mechanism. The Omicron variant consistently exhibited the weakest dextran-phase enrichment. Partition coefficients correlated strongly with hydrophobicity and isoelectric point, and obeyed a Collander-type relationship across polymer chemistries, enabling prediction of variant partitioning from a single reference measurement. Integrated upstream of an enzyme-linked oligonucleotide assay (ELONA), the optimized ATPS pre-concentration module enhanced detection sensitivity by 11.7-fold. This work establishes a generalizable, property-driven framework for the rational design of ATPS bioseparations and rapid adaptation to emerging pathogens.

title: In Silico Assessment of SYNGAP1 Missense Variant Pathogenicity.
authors: Ali, Aliaa E; Otranen, Henna-Riikka M; Lehtonen, Jukka V; Courtney, Michael J; Pentikainen, Olli T; Postila, Pekka A
abstract: SynGAP, a critical regulator at the postsynaptic density, is associated with Alzheimer's disease, tumorigenesis, and most notably, SYNGAP1-related disorders (SRD), which manifests as autism, epilepsy, and cognitive impairment. SRD is likely primarily caused by SynGAP missense (SGM) variants, whose pathogenicity is difficult to confirm experimentally. To address this issue, a wide range of structure- and/or sequence-based as well as machine learning- and deep learning-based in silico predictors were benchmarked against clinically annotated SRD data. Folding stability calculations (e.g., Foldetta) and deep learning methods ESM1b and AlphaMissense showed the highest prediction accuracy under default settings. Applying optimized nondefault thresholds, especially with AlphaMissense, could further improve predictor performance. The predictions exhibited a strong structural pattern: Pathogenic variants were highly enriched within defined structural domains, particularly the GAP and PH domains, whereas variants located in nondomain and nonmotif regions were predominantly predicted to be benign. The verified phosphosites and predicted phase separation impacting variants occupy matching sections, including the protein's N-terminal region and the vicinity of putative SH3-binding motif in the disordered regions. Thus, these regions collectively could act as phase separation-promoting segments, complementing the protein's trimerization-coupled coiled-coil domain. Finally, the SynGAP Missense (SGM) server was presented to support SynGAP variant assessment. The SGM server integrates a Data Table with top-performing predictors, a 3D Viewer for structure-level assessment and AI-generated lay summaries for all variants arising from single-base substitutions, including those not yet observed in public databases.

title: Drugging Pockets at the Surface of c-MYC Oncoproteins Revealed by Well-Tempered Metadynamics.
authors: Ge, Yanhong; Lu, Huixia; Marti, Jordi
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: The MYC oncogene encodes a master transcription factor essential for regulating cellular homeostasis, growth, and metabolism. However, its deregulation is involved in up to 70% of human cancers, where it drives uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Structurally, MYC is characterized by an N-terminal transactivation domain and a C-terminal bHLHLZ domain critical for DNA binding and dimerization with MAX. Despite its clinical significance, MYC has remained historically "undruggable" due to its intrinsically disordered structure and the absence of traditional binding pockets. In this study, we combined all-atom Molecular Dynamics and well-tempered metadynamics simulations to map the conformational landscape of a MYC motif in aqueous ionic solution. The selected energy-minimized structures exhibit stable conformations and drugging pockets, providing structural foundations for targetting c-MYC. Furthermore, both the electrostatic potential and docking results for the obtained structure and the MYC inhibitor's 10074-G5 demonstrated excellent fit, highlighting its potential as a drug target. This inhibitor, introduced in several previously unpublished drugging pockets, maintained a steady binding to MYC over unbiased trajectories lasting 1 mus. These findings provide a previously uncharacterized structural foundation for the design of innovative therapeutic interventions, such as small-molecule inhibitors or peptides aimed at disrupting oncogenic MYC activity.

title: FlexENN: A Graph Neural Network for Binding Energy Prediction of Globular and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins.
authors: Irshad, Maryum; Ori-McKenney, Kassandra; Dima, Ruxandra I
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) drive a large fraction of cellular signaling, transcription, and assembly through interfaces that often lack a defined geometry, making the prediction of their binding energies challenging for methods developed primarily for folded complexes. Here, we introduce FlexENN, an interface-focused message-passing graph neural network framework comprising two independently trained models: FlexENN-F for folded protein complexes and FlexENN-I for complexes containing a disordered partner. The FlexENN architecture constructs a local interface graph in which each residue node integrates the relative geometry, flexibility-related structural descriptors, and sequence information, allowing the network to learn structure-affinity relationships from a single resolved bound conformation. We also construct an IDP-containing dataset for training the FlexENN-I model. Benchmarked across folded complexes and IDP-containing systems, including tubulin-tubulin interfaces within microtubules (MTs) and MTs in complex with microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), with reference binding affinity values extracted from our experiments, the models reproduce physically reasonable energetic profiles, including the stronger interdimer relative to the lateral MT interactions, while feature-ablation analyses reveal system-dependent contributions of selected descriptors to the predictions. More broadly, this work delivers an accurate, structure-aware approach to predicting binding free energies for complexes of folded protein and complexes that contain ordered or partially ordered IDP regions for which a sufficiently well-defined bound structure is available.

title: Design of synthetic activators for programmable gene expression.
authors: Chen, Wei; Jiao, Ruopu; Coventry, Brian; Qu, Xiangli; Bauer, Magnus; Tran, Long; Tcheau, Tabitha; Wu, Kejia; Song, Zihao; Roullier, Nicole; Li, Xinting; Glasscock, Cameron; Hilton, Isaac B; Baker, David
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Transcription factors control gene expression by recruiting transcriptional coactivators through intrinsically disordered transcriptional activation domains (TADs), whose weak and promiscuous interactions make it difficult to establish quantitative relationships between coactivator recruitment and transcriptional output, and to precisely modulate gene expression. To overcome this limitation, we set out to design coactivator-recruiting proteins using AlphaFold3-predicted TAD-coactivator interactions as a guide. We developed a high-throughput functional screening platform in mammalian cells and identified over 300 well folded nanomolar affinity binders to the transcription coactivators Mediator (multiple subunits), BRD4, NCOA, and p300; targeted interface mutations enabled systematic tuning of their binding affinities. Using a panel of p300 binders spanning nanomolar to micromolar affinities, we found an ultrasensitive relationship between coactivator-binding affinity and transcriptional output, with a sharp transcriptional activation threshold at  approximately 500 nM. Incorporating p300 binder designs into CRISPRa yielded compact synthetic effectors that drove stronger activation than VPR across multiple genomic loci with minimal detectable cytotoxicity. Combining p300- and Mediator-specific binders further enhanced transcription, revealing functional synergy between these coactivators. Together, our work establishes a quantitative framework linking coactivator-binding affinity to transcriptional output and provides compact synthetic effectors for programmable gene activation.

title: So similar, yet so different: alpha-synuclein recognition of the isoform-specific VDAC protein-lipid interface.
authors: Rostovtseva, Tatiana K; Rajendran, Megha; Rosencrans, William M; Queralt-Martin, Maria; Wolfe, Mya S; Bautista, Nina A; Beyene, Bethel G; Larimi, Motahareh G; Sodt, Alexander J; Bezrukov, Sergey M
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: In mammals, VDAC exists as three isoforms - VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 - each characterized by a distinct tissue-dependent distribution and physiologic role. Isoform-specific knockout studies in cells and mice demonstrate distinct physiological roles for each VDAC isoform. The isoforms share about 70% sequence homology and a conserved beta-barrel structure and, when reconstituted into planar lipid membranes, form similar highly conductive, anion-selective, voltage-gated channels. A natural question, then, is how relatively minor differences in isoform sequences lead to striking differences in their interactions with protein partners and, consequently, in their physiological functions. To address this question, we used a small, intrinsically disordered cytosolic protein alpha-synuclein (alphaSyn) as a sensitive molecular probe. A comparative study with recombinant VDACs reconstituted into planar lipid membranes shows that, depending on the isoform, the alphaSyn-induced blockage exhibits up to 100-fold differences in on-rates and equilibrium constants. The isoforms also display distinct translocation regimes for alphaSyn, as evidenced by altered dependences of the off-rates on the applied voltage. Deletion of cysteine residues has a significant effect on alphaSyn binding. Combined with corresponding data obtained for VDAC2 substates - which show an order of magnitude variation in on-rates while maintaining the conserved equilibrium constants - and the results of molecular dynamics simulations, these findings point to a previously unrecognized step in VDAC inhibition by alphaSyn: an isoform-specific alphaSyn interaction with the VDAC protein-lipid interface. This finding opens a new paradigm for understanding VDAC isoform functions and developing isoform-specific therapeutics. NEW & NOTEWORTHY: Comparative analysis of alpha-synuclein interaction with three mammalian VDAC isoforms, complemented by corresponding data for VDAC2 substates and results from molecular dynamics simulations, reveals a new step in the chain of events leading to VDAC blockage. Specifically, our findings point to the isoform-specific interaction of alphaSyn with VDAC protein-lipid interface, thereby guiding a new strategy in the search for VDAC-targeting drugs.

title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
authors: Sarangthem Dinamani Singh; Gori Sankar Borah; Selvaraman Nagamani
abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.

title: DynamicsPLM: A Dynamics-Enriched Small Protein Language Model for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
authors: Tuan Minh Dao; Amarda Shehu; Anowarul Kabir
abstract: Predicting how mutations impact protein function and stability remains a key challenge in computational biology. Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

title: Nucleobase-Specific Recognition of DNA by Protamine
authors: Dhiman A; Mudiyanselage HE; Zhou H
abstract: Protamines—arginine (Arg)-rich, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)—replace histones to compact DNA in the sperm nucleus. While folded domains can bind DNA site-specifically, whether IDPs exhibit DNA-sequence specificity remains open. Here, we used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize protamine-DNA binding. Eight copies of salmon protamine (33 residues with 21 Arg) rapidly wrap around a 35-bp DNA molecule. In addition to salt bridges with DNA phosphates, Arg hydrogen-bonds with multiple nucleobases on both strands or the same strand. At the major groove, protamine prefers GC over AT by a 2.6-to-1 ratio, with guanine's O6 and N7 atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors; the preference is especially strong at G-tracts. This selectivity reverses at the minor groove, where AT overtakes GC by a 2.1-to-1 margin. The net effect is a moderate bias for GC over AT in protamine-base interactions. Additional simulations with 20-bp DNA molecules and free-energy calculations reinforce these observations. For experimental validation, we designed DNA sequences with 0–40% GC content. Protamine-DNA mixtures form aggregates, with an increasing propensity at higher GC content and upon shuffling into G-tracts. This work demonstrates that IDPs can bind DNA in a nucleobase-specific manner, with implications for protamine-mediated transcription silencing and remodeling of paternal chromatin.

title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
authors: Hamza Coban; Alfredo Alexander-Katz
abstract: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.

title: Fine-Tuning a Graph-Transformer ADMET Model Improves Half-Life and Plasma Protein Binding Concordance
authors: Basel Mansour; Chetan Anand P; Binil Benny; Sifat Ahmed; Shayoni Dutta; Daniel Kei Takahashi
abstract: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models are usually judged on predefined benchmark splits. Those splits are useful, but they do not show whether a model reproduces the pharmacokinetic (PK) numbers that are actually reported for individual drugs. Here we compared ADMET-AI with a fine-tuned NV-KERMT-70M-v2 model (“KERMT”) on the same Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC)-aligned endpoint definitions. KERMT was fine-tuned in two stages: a protocol check on the ChEMBL multitask (ChEMBL-MT) data set, then TDC-aligned regression and classification fine-tuning on merged ChEMBL, Biogen, ExpansionRx/OpenADMET and TDC data. Two retrospective literature comparisons were run. The first used a curated 25-drug oncology panel: for half-life (n = 17) KERMT cut mean absolute error (MAE) from 46.81 to 16.83 h (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0139, closer for 13 of 17 drugs); volume of distribution at steady state (VDss, n = 12) and hepatocyte clearance (n = 17) showed no statistically supported difference. The second, reported here for the first time, is an expanded three-way comparison of 53 oncology drugs × 3 endpoints (159 drug-endpoint rows) against curated literature and label values. On the 48 drugs with a usable half-life reference, KERMT more than halved the error (MAE 19.43 vs 43.38 h; median absolute error 12.01 vs 35.30 h; geometric mean fold error, GMFE, 2.72 vs 3.69; within 2-fold 41.0% vs 25.0%), was closer for 34 of 48 drugs (70.8%; 95% confidence interval, CI, 55.9-83.0%), and the paired Wilcoxon test was significant (p = 0.0002; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0004). The advantage persisted after each model's systematic bias was removed (p = 0.0004), so it is not a simple scale offset: ADMET-AI over-predicted half-life for 35 of 48 drugs (mean bias +29.20 h) whereas KERMT was mildly conservative (-13.79 h). For plasma protein binding ratio (PPBR, n = 21) KERMT had lower MAE (7.05 vs 9.44 percentage points) and the only statistically significant rank agreement with literature seen anywhere in this study (Spearman ρ = 0.540, p = 0.012, vs 0.400, p = 0.073), but the paired error difference was not significant (p = 0.157). One endpoint failed outright and we state it plainly: KERMT VDss predictions collapsed to near-baseline behaviour. They occupied a narrow band (46 of 53 drugs between 0 and 10 L/kg; standard deviation 3.64 vs 6.71 L/kg for ADMET-AI), no drug in the panel had an assay-matched VDss reference, and on the six drugs with an approximate reference the per-drug KERMT predictions (MAE 2.18 L/kg) were no better than replacing the entire model with one constant (MAE 2.14 L/kg) and worse than a no-information baseline (1.71 L/kg). KERMT VDss output should therefore not be used. A deliberately strict control bounds the positive findings as well: against a structure-blind constant predictor built by leave-one-out from the reference values, KERMT was statistically indistinguishable on both endpoints (half-life MAE 19.43 vs 16.07 h, p = 0.051; PPBR 7.05 vs 7.24 percentage points, p = 0.812), while ADMET-AI was significantly worse than that constant for half-life (p < 0.0001). We therefore make no claim of accurate numerical point prediction; the supported claims are that fine-tuning removes ADMET-AI's large systematic half-life error and that the PPBR rank correlation is compound-specific signal a constant cannot possess. Physically impossible values occurred in 16 of 159 KERMT rows and 21 of 159 ADMET-AI rows. Across 30 classification endpoints, mean inter-model Pearson correlation was 0.711 and mean binary agreement at 0.5 was 89%, which measures similarity, not accuracy. This version does not yet include official Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark-group evaluation of the fine-tuned models, replicate training seeds, or a training-set overlap audit; those gaps are declared explicitly rather than left implicit. The overall conclusion is endpoint-specific: fine-tuned KERMT is a materially better-calibrated half-life and plasma-protein-binding predictor than ADMET-AI on this panel, it is not yet a demonstrated ranking model for half-life, and its VDss head is unusable.
